title: Spring Lecture #14: How Java Web Apps Actually Work

questions.question: A browser opens `http://localhost:8080/hello`, and `HelloServlet` is mapped with `@WebServlet("/hello")`. Which statement matches the lecture's mental model?
options: Tomcat listens on port 8080, turns the HTTP text into request/response objects and calls the servlet mapped to `/hello`
`HelloServlet` opens a `ServerSocket` on port 8080 and waits for the browser itself
The browser loads the `HelloServlet` class and calls `doGet()` directly
The JVM's `main()` method receives every HTTP request and forwards it to `HelloServlet`
questions.explanation: The notes call "Servlet is listening on port 8080" a common beginner mistake: Tomcat is the long-running process that listens, parses HTTP, builds `HttpServletRequest`/`HttpServletResponse` and calls the matching servlet. The browser only speaks HTTP and knows nothing about Java classes.

questions.question: Why does the lecture's `pom.xml` declare `jakarta.servlet-api` with `<scope>provided</scope>`?
options: Because the Servlet API is only needed for unit tests, not for the application code
Because `provided` downloads the newest Servlet API automatically at runtime
Because the code needs it to compile, but Tomcat already supplies the Servlet API at runtime, so it must not be packaged in the WAR
Because WAR projects cannot contain any dependencies with the default scope
questions.explanation: `provided` means: available on the compile (and test) classpath, but expected from the container at runtime, so it is not bundled into `crud-app.war`. Tomcat's `lib` folder already has these classes. It is not test-only: `HttpServlet` is used by main code, which is exactly why compile access is required.

questions.question: The project has `<packaging>war</packaging>` and `<finalName>crud-app</finalName>`, and `UserServlet` is annotated `@WebServlet("/users")`. You copy `target/crud-app.war` into Tomcat's `webapps` folder and start Tomcat on 8080. Which URL reaches `UserServlet`?
options: `http://localhost:8080/users`
`http://localhost:8080/ServletCrudDemo/users`
`http://localhost:8080/webapps/crud-app/users`
`http://localhost:8080/crud-app/users`
questions.explanation: One external Tomcat can host several apps, so each WAR gets its own context path, taken from the WAR file name: `crud-app.war` is extracted to `webapps/crud-app` and served under `/crud-app`. The servlet mapping `/users` is appended after it. The artifactId is not used because `finalName` renamed the WAR, and `webapps` is a folder name, not part of the URL.
questions.source: notes p14-p19; Excalidraw p4-p5; code: pom.xml, UserServlet.java

questions.question: Tomcat starts with the default configuration (no load-on-startup). Then a browser sends `GET /hello` three times, and finally Tomcat is shut down. What does the console show from this servlet?
options: Constructor and init() printed when Tomcat starts, nothing per request, Destroy at shutdown
Constructor and init() printed once on the first request, then Destroy once at shutdown
Constructor and init() printed three times (once per request), then Destroy once
Constructor and init() printed three times, and Destroy printed after each request
questions.explanation: By default Tomcat creates the servlet lazily on the first matching request, calls `init()` once, and reuses that single object for later requests (only `service()`/`doGet()` run again, which print nothing here). `destroy()` runs once when the servlet is taken out of service, e.g. on shutdown. Creation at startup happens only if load-on-startup is configured.
questions.source: notes p13, p22-p28; code: HelloServlet.java; Excalidraw p5

questions.question: `HelloServlet` extends `HttpServlet` and overrides only `doGet()` (plus `init`/`destroy`). Postman sends `POST /crud-app/hello`. What happens and why?
options: `doGet()` runs, because a servlet with only one handler uses it for every HTTP method
Tomcat returns 404, because no servlet is mapped to `/hello` for POST
Tomcat throws an error at startup, because every `doXxx()` method must be overridden
`HttpServlet.service()` sees POST and calls the inherited default `doPost()`, which replies 405 Method Not Allowed
questions.explanation: `service()` runs for every request, checks the HTTP method and forwards to the matching `doXxx()`. Since `doPost()` is not overridden, the base implementation answers 405 Method Not Allowed. The URL mapping exists, so it is not a 404; mappings are by path, and the method check happens inside `service()`.

questions.question: `UserServlet` has `private UserService userService = new UserService();` and `UserService` stores users in a plain `HashMap`. Under a load test with many simultaneous `POST /users` requests, some users go missing. What is the underlying cause?
options: Tomcat uses one `UserServlet` instance for all requests and runs them on different threads, so the shared non-thread-safe `HashMap` is modified concurrently
Tomcat creates a new `UserServlet` per request, so each request writes to a different empty map
`HashMap` silently drops entries once it contains more than 16 users
The `provided` scope removes `UserService` from the WAR under heavy load
questions.explanation: The notes stress "one Servlet object -> many requests" and warn about instance variables. Each concurrent request runs on its own container thread against the same servlet and therefore the same `userDB` map, and `HashMap` is not safe for concurrent writes. A new instance per request is the misconception the lecture corrects; `HashMap` grows beyond its initial capacity of 16.

questions.question: A teammate says: "Spring Boot apps run with `java -jar` and serve requests on port 8080 without any Tomcat installed, so Spring Boot must have replaced servlets with its own HTTP server." How should you correct them?
options: They are right: Spring controllers open port 8080 themselves using `ServerSocket`
They are right: Spring Boot only uses servlets when the app is packaged as a WAR
Spring Boot embeds Tomcat inside the application (via the web starter); the servlet container still exists, it just starts from `main()`
Spring Boot converts each controller into a separate WAR that the JVM deploys automatically
questions.explanation: With external Tomcat the application goes inside the server; with Spring Boot the server starts inside the application when `SpringApplication.run()` runs. The notes say Spring Boot did not remove the servlet container concept, it made it easier to use: Tomcat is still there internally, and controllers never listen on ports themselves.

questions.question: Postman sends `POST /crud-app/users?name=Rahul&email=r@test.com&mobile=999` but forgets the `id` parameter. What does the client receive from the lecture's `doPost`?
options: 400 with `Some fields are missing`, because `id` is null
A 500 error: `Integer.parseInt(null)` throws `NumberFormatException` before the null check runs
201, because the user is created with id 0
201, because the user is created with a null id
questions.explanation: `getParameter("id")` returns null, and `Integer.parseInt(null)` throws `NumberFormatException` on the very first line. The exception escapes `doPost`, so Tomcat sends a 500 error page. The `id == null` check can never be true because parsing happens first; to fix it, read the raw string, check it for null, then parse.

questions.question: Now Postman sends `POST /crud-app/users?id=5&email=r@test.com&mobile=999` (no `name`). Assume nothing has been flushed to the client yet. What is the result?
options: 400 with only the "Some fields are missing" message; the user is not stored
500, because `new User(...)` rejects a null name
400 with both messages; the user is stored with a null name
201 with both messages in the body, and user 5 is stored with a null name
questions.explanation: The `if` block writes the error but has no `return`, so execution continues: the user (name null) is put in the map, then `setStatus(201)` overwrites the 400 because the response is not yet committed, and the success JSON is appended after the error JSON. Adding `return;` after the 400 branch fixes it. The `User` constructor just assigns fields, so null is accepted.

questions.question: In the servlet project, `/users`, `/products` and `/orders` would need `UserServlet`, `ProductServlet` and `OrderServlet`. In a Spring MVC app, three `@RestController` classes handle the same paths. Which servlet(s) does Tomcat call for these requests?
options: One central `DispatcherServlet` for all of them, which then picks the matching controller method
Three servlets that Spring generates automatically, one per `@RestController` class
No servlet at all: Spring MVC bypasses the servlet API and calls controllers from Tomcat's connector
One servlet per `@GetMapping`/`@PostMapping` method, created when the method is first called
questions.explanation: Spring MVC is built on the servlet API: Tomcat calls a single front servlet, `DispatcherServlet`, for incoming requests, and it checks Spring MVC's mappings to choose the controller method. Controllers are ordinary beans, not servlets, so Spring does not generate a servlet per controller or per method.
